You're touching on the topic the correct way and with the correct group in question, but saying the Germans weren't "done fighting" is only right in certain contemporary political circles.

While fighting stopped with the 11/11/18 armistice, the war didn't officially end before the signing of what perhaps is the reason for WW2: The Treaty of Versailles (and the subsequent treaties)

The Versailles Treaty was written largely by British, French and US leaders all of whom had certain opinions on Germany's role was and should be in Europe at the time.
Some, like France, wanted guarantees that Germany would never be in a position to start a war ever again, so the treaty was very strict in regards to German military strength, eg. limiting its army to «no more than 100,000 men».
Furthermore, the treaty singled out Germany to be made fiscally responsible for the whole war. This, added to the consequences of how the German government decided to fund the war (loans and not taxation), would the biggest factors in what lead to the hyperinflation of the Mark in the first half of the 20's, and when people go hungry they want it to be blamed on someone.

Looking at this in both local and global perspectives of hegemony, it wouldn't be wrong saying the Treaty of Versailles was designed to keep German power checkmated and this is exactly how the political right viewed it.

Now what you wrote about Germans weren't 'done fighting' is partly correct as it was only the political right who held this belief that Germany hadn't really lost the war at all and could keep fighting, while what they called the Stab in the back myth was central to the Nazi political stance it was still a myth.

Also, it's very important to note that in addition to traditional and rising nationalism (fueled by the hyperinflation of 1921-24), antisemitism was and had been prevalent in Europe for a long time in various degrees: As an emphasis to this point, the last sentence to the second paragraph to Norway's constitution of 1814 explicitly forbade Jews, Jesuits and monks entrance to the Kingdom of Norway. The second paragraph!

For Germany at the time: During the war, German socialist movements were (for different reasons) protesting the war which in turn led to rising resentment by the German right towards communism and socialism, "the mortal enemies of Nazism". Jews were also blamed for issues during the war, such as strikes within arms-industry factories which were seen as weakening the war effort. So when a Jewish-led communist group appeared (in Hitlers Munich) after the war, the already resented socialists were naturally connected to the already disliked Jews

So in post-WWI Germany, Jews basically got blamed for the German defeat in WWI and thus the state of post-war Germany because of a mix of rising nationalism added to a prevalence of antisemitism in European culture and then the perceived connection between socialism and Jews; as opposed to what the reality was:

The war was lost when Germany's allies started capitulating, a war-weary population wanted out, and then through the treaties: Germany's greedy competitors in the world of geopolitical hegemony wanted to make sure Germany couldn't get back on its feet and compete for control in both Europe and other continents
